
  The modern computer keyboard took shape in the early 1980s. IBM's Personal Computer, released in 1981, shipped with a keyboard that many users remember fondly. Its successor, the Model M, introduced in 1984, used a
  buckling-spring mechanism, in which each key pressed a small metal spring that gave a distinct tactile feel and an audible click. Many enthusiasts still regard it as one of the finest keyboards ever made. Around the
  same time, the Cherry Corporation developed the MX switch, which used a stem that moved vertically through a plastic housing and a metal contact that closed the circuit. Cherry's switches became the foundation of much
  of the mechanical keyboard market, and their variants, distinguished by color and force, are still widely sold.

  Not every design followed the mechanical path. Membrane keyboards, which use layers of flexible plastic and printed circuits, became cheap and common in the 1980s and dominated consumer machines, because they were
  quiet and inexpensive to manufacture. Laptops moved to scissor-style mechanisms, where two crossed plastic arms guided each key, allowing very thin profiles. Touch screens and virtual keyboards have spread onto phones
  and tablets, but they have not eliminated the physical keyboard, in part because touch typing depends on the feedback that a physical key provides.

  Looking back, the keyboard's history is a story of inherited habits. Its layout reflects a jam that was solved long ago, its mechanisms reflect decades of engineering refinement, and its basic promise, that a person
  can press a key and produce a precise symbol, has held steady since the first typewriter. Few tools have carried so much of their past forward so faithfully.
